questions.question: Eight months after working a fatal apartment fire where two children died, an EMT still has nightmares about the scene, avoids driving past the building, and startles badly at the sound of a smoke alarm. What stress disorder best fits this picture?
questions.explanation: The symptoms are a delayed reaction to a prior incident, appearing and persisting long after the event itself.

questions.question: A paramedic who treated victims of a mass shooting two years ago reports intrusive memories, emotional numbness, and trouble sleeping that have never fully gone away despite peer support. What condition should be suspected?
questions.explanation: Unresolved reactions tied to an earlier traumatic incident that involved harm and threat of harm point to PTSD.

questions.question: During a routine physical, a firefighter mentions that ever since a building collapse early in his career he has flashbacks when he hears a PASS alarm and has started drinking to sleep. What delayed stress reaction is this?
questions.explanation: Flashbacks and avoidance surfacing long after a life-threatening incident are hallmarks of PTSD.

questions.question: A veteran EMT notices that over the past year she has stopped introducing herself to patients, feels irritated by minor complaints, and no longer feels anything when a patient cries. Her empathy has slowly drained away. What is this called?
questions.explanation: The gradual loss of compassion after repeated exposure to others' suffering is the defining feature of compassion fatigue.

questions.question: After months of back-to-back overdose and cardiac arrest calls, a paramedic tells his partner, 'I used to care about these people. Now I just go through the motions.' What stress disorder is developing?
questions.explanation: Caring capacity erodes gradually with cumulative exposure, which is compassion fatigue rather than a single-incident reaction.

questions.question: A charge nurse reviewing survey results finds her long-serving EMS crews score lower on empathy measures every year they stay in the field. What phenomenon do the surveys describe?
questions.explanation: Compassion fatigue builds over time with years of caregiving, and studies show it rises with experience.

questions.question: An EMT who was energized by busy shifts last year now dreads the tones, has stomach aches before work, and snaps at her family after hard calls. The job's demands have become a harmful burden rather than a challenge. What type of stress response is she showing?
questions.explanation: Her response to the stressor is negative and damaging, which is distress rather than beneficial eustress.

questions.question: After a week of short staffing and mandatory overtime, a paramedic reports headaches, poor sleep, and a feeling of being overwhelmed that is hurting his performance. What is this negative response to a stressor called?
questions.explanation: The stressor is producing a harmful, negative response in the provider, the definition of distress.

questions.question: Two EMTs work the same difficult pediatric call. One feels focused and motivated afterward; the other feels shaky, tearful, and unable to concentrate for the rest of the shift. Which EMT is experiencing distress?
choices: an acute stress reaction (the first EMT)
questions.explanation: Distress is the negative response to a stressor; the same event can produce eustress in one person and distress in another.

questions.question: After a call, an EMT realizes the patient's blood got into a cut on her hand. She fills out an exposure report and calls the one person in her department responsible for verifying the exposure and contacting the hospital for the source patient's test results. Who is she calling?
questions.explanation: Managing exposures and infection control follow-up for the department is the designated officer's assigned role.

questions.question: A hospital diagnoses a transported patient with meningitis two days after the call and must notify the transporting EMS agency. Under the Ryan White notification process, the hospital communicates with which person at the agency?
questions.explanation: The designated officer is the department's official point of contact for exposure notification and infection control.

questions.question: Your department is writing its exposure control plan and must name the individual who will track crew exposures, arrange postexposure follow-up, and serve as liaison with medical facilities. What position must be named?
questions.explanation: Federal law and OSHA practice place exposure management and infection control responsibility on a named designated officer.

questions.question: Your crew is dispatched to a nursing home where 14 residents developed vomiting and diarrhea a day after the same catered lunch. The suspected route of spread is a contaminated meal. What type of transmission is this?
questions.explanation: Illness caused by an organism contaminating food is foodborne transmission.

questions.question: At a summer camp, dozens of children become ill with bloody diarrhea after eating undercooked burgers at a cookout. Investigators trace the bacteria to the ground beef. How was the organism transmitted?
questions.explanation: The pathogen reached the patients through contaminated food, the definition of foodborne transmission.

questions.question: A city issues a boil-water order after E. coli is found in the municipal supply, and your station begins running calls for dehydrated elderly patients with gastroenteritis. What transmission route is involved?
questions.explanation: The definition covers contamination of food or water with a disease-causing organism.

questions.question: An EMT starts a station routine of exercising on shift, keeping regular sleep hours on days off, getting an annual physical, and attending a peer support night each month. What concept is she practicing?
questions.explanation: Wellness is the active pursuit of good health, and her routine deliberately pursues physical and mental health.

questions.question: Your department replaces a punitive fitness test with voluntary health screenings, nutrition coaching, and on-duty workout time, aiming to keep crews healthy across a whole career. What is the program's focus?
questions.explanation: The program actively pursues a state of good health rather than just treating illness or injury.

questions.question: A paramedic who smokes decides to quit, joins a cessation program, and tracks his blood pressure monthly with the department nurse. Which idea best describes what he is doing?
questions.explanation: Quitting smoking and monitoring his health are deliberate actions in pursuit of good health, which is wellness.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: A delayed stress reaction to a prior incident. Often the result of one or more unresolved issues concerning the incident, and may relate to an incident that involved physical harm or the threat of physical harm.
questions.explanation: posttraumatic stress disorder: A delayed stress reaction to a prior incident. Often the result of one or more unresolved issues concerning the incident, and may relate to an incident that involved physical harm or the threat of physical harm.

questions.question: What does the term "posttraumatic stress disorder" mean?
choices: Reactions to stress that occur after a stressful situation.

A delayed stress reaction to a prior incident. Often the result of one or more unresolved issues concerning the incident, and may relate to an incident that involved physical harm or the threat of physical harm.
Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) is caused by HIV, which damages the cells in the body's immune system so that the body is unable to fight infection or certain cancers.
The way in which an infectious disease is spread: contact, airborne, by vehicles, or by vectors.
questions.explanation: posttraumatic stress disorder: A delayed stress reaction to a prior incident. Often the result of one or more unresolved issues concerning the incident, and may relate to an incident that involved physical harm or the threat of physical harm.

questions.question: After the September 11, 2001 attacks, FDNY firefighters and EMS responders worked rescue and recovery at Ground Zero. Federal monitoring later found nearly 20% of responders were diagnosed with World Trade Center-related PTSD, and about half of the mental health disorders did not appear until 11 to 13 years after the exposure. What does this case illustrate about PTSD in responders?
choices: PTSD only develops in responders who showed obvious symptoms at the scene.
A single critical incident debriefing held right after the event is enough to prevent PTSD.
Responders who stay busy and avoid talking about the event rarely develop PTSD.
PTSD can be a delayed reaction that surfaces years after the incident, so responders need monitoring and follow-up long after the event, not just in the weeks after it.
questions.explanation: PTSD is a delayed stress reaction; symptoms may emerge years after the traumatic incident.

questions.question: Two bombs exploded near the Boston Marathon finish line on April 15, 2013, killing 3 spectators and wounding more than 260 people. Medical tent volunteers and responders treated severe blast injuries, including many amputations. Ten years later, responders still described intrusive thoughts, nightmares, and anxiety, and a hospital support group was treating classic PTSD symptoms. What is the main lesson of this case?
choices: Only responders who were physically injured at the scene are at risk for lasting PTSD.
Symptoms lasting more than a year mean the responder was unfit for duty from the start.
PTSD after a mass-casualty event resolves on its own once the responder returns to a normal schedule.
Even after a well-run, successful response, PTSD symptoms can persist for years, so planned long-term follow-up matters as much as the initial debriefing.
questions.explanation: PTSD is a delayed, persistent reaction that can follow even a single well-handled incident.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: A stress disorder characterized by gradual lessening of compassion over time.
questions.explanation: compassion fatigue: A stress disorder characterized by gradual lessening of compassion over time.

questions.question: What does the term "compassion fatigue" mean?
choices: A situation in which a person has had contact with blood, body fluids, tissues, or airborne particles and has the potential to develop a disease.
What airborne bacterial disease is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, spreads when an infected person coughs or sneezes, and is indicated by a positive skin test showing exposure to the bacterium.
A stress disorder characterized by gradual lessening of compassion over time.
A microorganism that is capable of causing disease in a susceptible host.
questions.explanation: compassion fatigue: A stress disorder characterized by gradual lessening of compassion over time.

questions.question: During the COVID-19 pandemic, a Spanish study of 506 healthcare professionals used the ProQOL scale to measure professional quality of life after months of caring for dying patients. It found 60.4% of respondents had high levels of compassion fatigue and another 33.6% had moderate levels. What pattern does this case show?
choices: Compassion fatigue develops gradually as compassion erodes over months of caring for suffering patients, and it should be treated as a measurable occupational injury, not an attitude problem.
Compassion fatigue is a sudden reaction to one especially bad call.
High compassion fatigue scores simply mean the clinicians chose the wrong profession.
Only new, inexperienced clinicians are at risk of losing compassion for patients.
questions.explanation: Compassion fatigue is the gradual lessening of compassion over time with sustained caregiving.

questions.question: A New Zealand journal review of international evidence on compassion fatigue in paramedics found that its prevalence increases the longer a provider spends in the role. Job satisfaction, education, and regular monitoring of mental health were identified as key protectors. Based on this case, what should an EMS agency do?
choices: Because compassion fatigue rises with years spent in the role, the agency should use routine mental health check-ins, manageable workloads, and job satisfaction measures as frontline defenses.
The agency should rotate providers permanently out of patient care after five years.
Because it mainly affects new hires, the agency should focus support only during the first year.
Because compassion fatigue cannot be monitored, the agency should wait until a provider resigns.
questions.explanation: Compassion steadily lessens across a caregiving career, so ongoing monitoring and workload management are key defenses.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: A negative response to a stressor.
questions.explanation: distress: A negative response to a stressor.

questions.question: What does the term "distress" mean?
choices: The spread of an organism via droplets or dust.
A negative response to a stressor.
The use of objects to limit a person's ability to see you.
The individual in the department who is charged with the responsibility of managing exposures and infection control.
questions.explanation: distress: A negative response to a stressor.

questions.question: Beyond Blue's 'Answering the Call' survey collected responses from 21,014 current and former Australian police and emergency services personnel. One in three employees reported high or very high psychological distress, and employees with more than 10 years of service were almost twice as likely to experience it. What is the main lesson for EMS agencies?
choices: Distress accumulates with years of service, so agencies should measure it routinely instead of waiting for a crisis.
Because distress is a personal response, agencies have no reason to track it.
Distress only appears after a single catastrophic incident.
Distress is rare in emergency services and mainly affects new recruits.
questions.explanation: Distress, the negative response to stressors, builds with cumulative exposure over a career.

questions.question: After the April 19, 1995 bombing of the Murrah Federal Building in Oklahoma City, which killed 168 people, researchers interviewed 255 survivors about six months later. They found 45% had a postdisaster psychiatric disorder, while many others were distressed and hyperaroused without meeting criteria for an illness. What should providers expect after a critical incident?
choices: Responders who do not develop a disorder were not really affected by the event.
Only people who meet criteria for a psychiatric disorder need support after an incident.
Distress is the common response after a critical incident, so support should be normalized for all responders and survivors, not only those with a diagnosed disorder.
Distress after a disaster is a sign of poor training and should be documented as such.
questions.explanation: Distress affects far more people than those who develop a formal disorder after an incident.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The individual in the department who is charged with the responsibility of managing exposures and infection control.
questions.explanation: designated officer: The individual in the department who is charged with the responsibility of managing exposures and infection control.

questions.question: What does the term "designated officer" mean?
choices: The individual in the department who is charged with the responsibility of managing exposures and infection control.

What are the hazards at a structure fire that include possible building collapse, high heat, smoke and toxic gases, and oxygen-deficient air, and that require EMTs to stage at a safe distance and stay clear until the fire department declares the scene safe.
The capacity of an individual to cope with and recover from distress.
The most effective way to preserve body heat when functioning in cold, wet weather — wearing at least three layers of clothing.
questions.explanation: designated officer: The individual in the department who is charged with the responsibility of managing exposures and infection control.

questions.question: Congress passed the Ryan White CARE Act in 1990. Its responder provisions required emergency response employers to name a designated officer for exposure questions, and hospitals were required to tell that officer whether a source patient had a listed infectious disease. Why does this designated officer role matter?
choices: The designated officer personally treats every exposed provider at the hospital.
The designated officer is the department's official channel for exposure notification, which is what makes hospitals share source-patient results with the agency.
The designated officer role exists mainly to discipline providers who skip PPE.
Any crew member can call the hospital directly and get a source patient's test results.
questions.explanation: Exposure follow-up runs through the designated officer, the person charged with managing exposures and infection control.

questions.question: CDC interim Ebola guidance for EMS systems and 911 centers states that any provider whose skin or mucous membranes contact a suspected Ebola patient's fluids should act immediately, and directs the provider to report the exposure to a supervisor or designated infection control officer as soon as possible. What should the exposed EMT do?
choices: Stop work at once, wash the exposed area, and report the exposure to a supervisor or the designated infection control officer as soon as possible.
Handle the follow-up personally by calling the hospital laboratory for the patient's results.
Wait to see whether the patient tests positive before reporting anything.
Finish the transport, then mention the exposure at the end of the shift if symptoms develop.
questions.explanation: After any exposure: stop, wash, and notify the designated officer immediately, not at the end of shift.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The contamination of food or water with an organism that can cause disease.
questions.explanation: foodborne transmission: The contamination of food or water with an organism that can cause disease.

questions.question: What does the term "foodborne transmission" mean?
choices: The organism or individual that is attacked by the infecting agent.
The active pursuit of a state of good health.
The abnormal invasion of a host or host tissues by organisms such as bacteria, viruses, or parasites, with or without signs or symptoms of disease.
The contamination of food or water with an organism that can cause disease.
questions.explanation: foodborne transmission: The contamination of food or water with an organism that can cause disease.

questions.question: In 1993, E. coli O157:H7 in undercooked hamburger patties from Jack in the Box restaurants sickened 732 people across four western states. Four children died and 178 people were left with permanent injury, including kidney and brain damage. What is the key lesson for EMTs from this outbreak?
choices: Clusters of bloody diarrhea in children after eating out should be reported quickly, because early recognition of foodborne transmission helps stop outbreaks.
Undercooked food only causes mild illness, so clusters of cases do not need urgent reporting.
Bloody diarrhea after a meal is usually caused by airborne spread inside the restaurant.
Food histories are not useful on GI calls because hospitals identify outbreaks on their own.
questions.explanation: Contaminated food is a classic vehicle for foodborne transmission, and clusters are the clue that links cases into an outbreak.

questions.question: In 2011, Listeria monocytogenes on whole cantaloupes from Jensen Farms in Colorado infected 147 people in 28 states. Thirty-three people died, most of them elderly, and one pregnant patient miscarriage. CDC called it the deadliest US foodborne outbreak in decades. What should EMTs keep in mind from this case?
choices: Listeriosis only causes mild stomach upset and never affects pregnant patients.
Produce cannot transmit disease, so fever in an elderly patient after eating melon is unrelated to food.
Elderly and pregnant patients with fever and confusion after suspect food should have listeriosis considered, since foodborne illness can be deadly in these groups.
Foodborne outbreaks stay local, so a nationally distributed product is not a concern for EMS.
questions.explanation: A single contaminated food item distributed nationally shows how far foodborne transmission can reach before it is detected.

questions.question: Which term is defined as: The active pursuit of a state of good health.
questions.explanation: wellness: The active pursuit of a state of good health.

questions.question: What does the term "wellness" mean?
choices: Exposure or transmission of a communicable disease from one person to another by physical contact.
The active pursuit of a state of good health.
The spread of an organism via droplets or dust.
What PPE must be worn when blood or body fluids may splash into the eyes, noting that prescription glasses do not provide adequate protection because they offer little or no side protection.
questions.explanation: wellness: The active pursuit of a state of good health.

questions.question: In 1997 the IAFF and IAFC launched the Fire Service Joint Labor Management Wellness-Fitness Initiative, built together by ten metropolitan departments and their unions, including FDNY, Seattle, Phoenix, and LA County. The program is mandatory in structure but non-punitive, covering medical exams, fitness, rehabilitation, and behavioral health. What makes this wellness model work?
choices: Wellness works when labor and management build the program together and keep it non-punitive, as an organized, career-long pursuit of good health.
A wellness program only needs to cover fitness testing once, at hiring.
Wellness is an individual responsibility, so departments should not organize programs.
Wellness programs work best when failing a fitness test leads to discipline.
questions.explanation: Wellness is the active pursuit of good health, best pursued as an organized, non-punitive system.

questions.question: NFPA counted 62 on-duty firefighter deaths in the United States in 2024. Overexertion and strain caused 40 of them, and 30 of those were heart attacks; US Fire Administration guidance notes sudden cardiac events account for nearly 45% of firefighter line-of-duty deaths in recent years. What is the main lesson of these statistics?
choices: On-duty deaths are mainly caused by trauma, so health screening is a low priority.
Because sudden cardiac events are the leading killer of firefighters, fitness, sleep, and medical screening are life-safety equipment, and wellness is a safety program.
Wellness only matters for older firefighters nearing retirement.
Cardiac deaths are unavoidable in the fire service, so screening has little value.
questions.explanation: The leading killer of firefighters is a health condition, which is why wellness, the active pursuit of good health, is a safety program.
